bullets.text: Energy source for the remote will be a battery, agreed as the most cost-effective option.
Design will use chip on print for the electronics.
Case design will be bright, colorful, trendy, compact and strong.
User interface will use simple push buttons rather than scroll wheels, to keep costs down.
Speech/voice recognition will be tentatively included as a 'supplement' feature, pending further cost research from the industrial engineer.

Next steps assigned: look-and-feel design, user interface design (working with clay prototype together with the industrial engineer), and a product evaluation by the marketing expert, all due before the next meeting in 30 minutes.
The industrial engineer expressed doubt about how well voice/speech recognition would work, since different people have different voices and the system would need training.
The marketing expert cautioned that having too many advertised features could confuse consumers, so only one or two standout features should be highlighted.
The marketing expert noted the team needs to reach market ahead of competitors, especially before the Christmas season.
How expensive/feasible the speech recognition feature would actually be, to be researched by the industrial engineer before finalizing.
Exact meaning and scope of 'supplements' in the interface concept was initially unclear to the project manager.
Industrial engineer disagreed with using scroll wheels, noting they require a more sophisticated (pricier) chip compared to simple push buttons, favoring buttons for cost reasons.
Marketing expert found the oversized 'impossible to misplace' remote design impractical/funny, disagreeing it would work as an impulse purchase item.
Done: Recapped the previous meeting's findings on user needs, marketing approach, technical features, and interface ideas
Done: Confirmed agreement from the group that the recap matched the prior discussion
Next: Led the group to decide on the concept—agreed on battery power, chip on print, and a trendy, compact, strong case
Next: Assigned Francina and the industrial engineer to build a prototype together using modeling clay, with the marketing expert to do product evaluation
Next: Scheduled the next meeting in thirty minutes and directed participants to contact coaches with questions
Done: Presented interface concepts including on/off, channel lock, swap/next channel buttons, volume, subtitles, color/contrast controls, memory and mute buttons
Done: Proposed a speech/voice recognition feature as the standout innovation, where the remote learns the user's voice to trigger functions like channel switching
Done: Showed example remotes (multipurpose voice-recognition remote, child-friendly remote, oversized 'impossible to lose' remote) to illustrate design options
Next: Reiterated her personal preference for incorporating speech recognition into the final design
Blocker: Industrial engineer expressed doubt about how well voice recognition would work across different users' voices
Done: Presented technical components needed: case (durable, recyclable plastic), integrated circuit, resistor, capacitor, diode, transistor, resonator, battery, circuit board
Done: Recommended a rechargeable battery to lower long-term cost and suggested alternative energy sources like kinetic/dynamo or solar cells
Done: Explained how the remote works internally, from button press to Morse code signal generation to infrared transmission
Done: Showed physical remote control internals (chip, resistors, transistor, capacitor, diode) and circuit board printing process
Done: Recommended push buttons over scroll wheels to keep chip costs down
Next: Tasked with researching the cost/feasibility of implementing speech recognition
Next: Assigned to work with Francina on a modeling clay prototype for look and feel
Done: Presented market research method—reviewing competitor ads, browsing online, and observing/asking about remotes people already own
Done: Reported findings that consumers prefer small, simple designs with few obvious-function buttons and an eye-catching look
Done: Advised getting to market before competitors and narrowing the product's marketed features to just one or two standout selling points
Done: Noted current design trend toward fruit/vegetable shapes and soft, spongy materials over hard plastic or metal
Next: Suggested speech recognition could serve as the product's star marketable feature, pending cost research
Next: Tasked with producing a product evaluation for the next phase
Assigned to develop the look-and-feel design and work with the industrial engineer on a prototype using modeling clay before the next meeting (in thirty minutes)
To research and report back on how expensive speech recognition would be to implement
Assigned to come up with the user interface design and work with Francina on a prototype using modeling clay before the next meeting
Assigned to work on the product evaluation before the next meeting
Will reconvene the meeting in thirty minutes per the project timetable
Available (along with the coaches) to answer any questions during the individual action phase
Specific instructions for the modeling clay prototype work will be sent by coaches to the relevant participants
Whether to include speech recognition as a core feature remains pending further cost research, since concerns were raised about recognizing different users' voices
Final decision on which one or two standout features to emphasize in marketing (per the marketing expert's suggestion) was not concluded
Team reviewed prior meeting's requirements, then heard three presentations: UI concepts (Francina), components/technical design (S3), and marketing findings (S2).
Group converged on a concept: battery-powered, chip-on-print circuit, push buttons (not scroll wheels), bright/colorful/compact/trendy/strong casing.
Speech/voice recognition was tentatively chosen as the product's standout feature, pending cost research.
Decided on battery as energy source over other options, agreed as most cost-effective.
Agreed to use push buttons instead of scroll wheels to avoid needing a more sophisticated (pricier) chip.
Agreed on case direction: bright, colorful, compact, trendy design, and strong/durable material.
Tentatively selected speech recognition as the marketed 'star feature,' contingent on further cost investigation by the industrial engineer.
S3 raised doubts about voice recognition feasibility (per-person voice variation, training required), needs further technical/cost research before finalizing.
Marketing expert (S2) stressed narrowing to only 1-2 headline features to avoid confusing consumers — final feature set not yet locked down.
Next meeting in 30 minutes: Francina and Jana (industrial engineer) must build a prototype using modeling clay per coach instructions; marketing expert to deliver product evaluation.
